body.p: Claims 1-22 are pending. Claims 1, 3, 4, 11, 12, 13, 15, and 20-22 are amended. No new matter has been added.
Summary of Examiner Interview

Applicant thanks the Examiner for the courtesies extended during an Examiner interview conductor with Nishitkumar V. Patel, the undersigned, on October 18, 2024. During the interview, claim 1 was discussed in view of Taylor et al. (US Pre-Grant Publication 2019/0392641 Al) ("Taylor") and in view of section 112 rejections below. Details of the interview are provided below. The teleconference furthered prosecution.
Claim Rejection - 35 USC § 102

Claims 1, 2, 11, 12, 14, 20 and 21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Taylor et al. (US Pre-Grant Publication 2019/0392641 Al) ("Taylor"). This rejection is respectfully traversed.

It has not been shown that Taylor discloses the recitations of claim 1. For example, it has not been shown that Taylor discloses "rendering, in a virtual environment, a first virtual object having the type of material of the real-world object; and providing the set of audio data to be output as sound when the first virtual object in the virtual environment interacts with a second virtual object in the virtual environment", as is recited in claim 1. It is stated on page
4 of the office action that:

As stated in paragraph 57 of Taylor, "input sound can be ... modified" and "played on one or more speakers .. . at the appropriate time, e.g., as a virtual object is emulated to strike the real-world object for which the sound is tailored". It has not been shown that paragraph 57 discloses that the virtual object of Taylor has "the type of material of the real-world object", as is recited in claim 1.

It is stated in paragraph 58 of Taylor that "the correlations described above may be dynamically generated using audio manipulations and customized reverberation". Again, it has not been shown that paragraph 58 discloses that the virtual object of Taylor has "the type of material of the real-world object", as is recited in claim 1.

Paragraph 59 of Taylor states that "SLAM maps" are used "to identify whether the virtual object interacts with the real-world object, e.g., at an oblique angle or direct angle according to the example above". Again, it has not been shown that paragraph 59 discloses that the virtual object of Taylor has "the type of material of the real-world object", as is recited in claim 1.

Paragraph 60 of Taylor describes that "a tester may bounce real world objects later to be emulated by virtual objects off certain known materials to record the initial sound profiles, which are associated with the known materials in a data structure". As such, again, it has not
been shown that any of the "virtual objects" in paragraph 60 of Taylor has "the type of material of the real-world object", as is recited in claim 1.
Paragraph 61 of Taylor states that "transform functions may be implemented for

different types of materials such as wood, metal, etc. and for specific object types if desired". Thus, it has not been shown that paragraph 61 discloses that the virtual object of Taylor has "the type of material of the real-world object", as is recited in claim 1. Hence, it has not been shown that Taylor discloses "rendering, in a virtual environment, a first virtual object having the type of material of the real-world object; and providing the set of audio data to be output as sound when the first virtual object in the virtual environment interacts with a second virtual object in the virtual environment", as is recited in claim 1.

In addition, Taylor describes in paragraph 57 that "a virtual object is emulated to strike the real-world object". As such, it has not been shown that the real-world object of Taylor is "a second virtual object in the virtual environment", as is recited in claim 1. Hence, for the reasons set forth above, claim 1 is submitted to be novel in view of Taylor.
Moreover, for the same reasons set forth above, independent claims 11 and 20 are

submitted to be novel in view of Taylor. For example, for the same reasons set forth above, it has not been shown that Taylor discloses a processor configured to "provide the type of material to a client device to facilitate a display, in a virtual environment, of a first virtual object having the type of material of the real-world object; and provide the set of audio data to be output as sound when the first virtual object interacts with a second virtual object in the virtual environment", as is recited in claim 11. As another example, for the same reasons set forth above, it has not been shown that Taylor discloses a server configured to "provide the type of material to facilitate a display, in a virtual environment, of a first virtual object having the type of material of the real-world object; and provide the set of audio data to be output as sound when the first virtual object interacts with a second virtual object in the virtual environment", as is recited in claim 20. Hence, for the reasons set forth above, claims 11 and 20 are submitted to be novel in view of Taylor.
Claim 2 depends from independent claim 1, claims 12 and 14 depend from
independent claim 11, and claim 21 depends from independent claim 20. Hence, for the same
reasons set forth above with respect to independent claims 1, 11, and 20, the dependent claims 2, 12, 14, and 21 are submitted to be novel in view of Taylor.
Thus, it is respectfully requested that the section 102 rejection of claims 1, 2, 11, 12, 14, 20 and 21 be withdrawn.
Claim Rejection - 35 USC § 103
Claims 3 to 10, 13, 15 to 19, and 22 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Taylor. This rejection is respectfully traversed.

Claims 3-10 depend from independent claim 1. It has not been shown that Taylor discloses or suggests the recitations of claim 1. For example, for the same reasons set forth above, it has not been shown that Taylor discloses or suggests "rendering, in a virtual environment, a first virtual object having the type of material of the real-world object; and providing the set of audio data to be output as sound when the first virtual object in the virtual environment interacts with a second virtual object in the virtual environment", as is recited in claim 1. Hence, claim 1 and dependent claims 3-10 are submitted to be nonobvious over Taylor.

Claims 13 and 15-19 depend from independent claim 11. It has not been shown that Taylor discloses or suggests the recitations of claim 11. For example, for the same reasons set forth above, it has not been shown that Taylor discloses a processor configured to "provide the type of material to a client device to facilitate a display, in a virtual environment, of a first virtual object having the type of material of the real-world object; and provide the set of audio data to be output as sound when the first virtual object interacts with a second virtual object in the virtual environment", as is recited in claim 11. Thus, claim 11 and dependent claims 13 and 15-19 are submitted to be nonobvious over Taylor.

Claim 22 depends from independent claim 20. It has not been shown that Taylor discloses or suggests the recitations of claim 20. For example, for the same reasons set forth above, it has not been shown that Taylor discloses a server configured to "provide the type of material to facilitate a display, in a virtual environment, of a first virtual object having the type of material of the real-world object; and provide the set of audio data to be output as

sound when the first virtual object interacts with a second virtual object in the virtual environment", as is recited in claim 20. Therefore, claim 20 and dependent claim 22 are submitted to be nonobvious over Taylor.
Traversal of Official Notice
It is stated on pages 6-7 of the office action that:

As to Claims 8, 9, and 19: Taylor already discloses to adapt audio characteristics of a virtual abject depending on the type of detected material (see Paras. 52-54). Adapting other characteristics of the virtual object (such as haptics) to the detected material is well known in the art (see e.g. DS, para.
54), and would be considered by the skilled person when starting from Taylor. Therefore, the subject matter of these claims would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the
art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
(Emphasis Added). This statement is respectfully traversed.
An identity of the reference "DS, para. 54" is not clear. In the Office Action, the
Examiner has rejected the claims in view of Taylor as a reference. Paragraph 54 of Taylor is reproduced below.
[0054] Likewise, the base sound may be modified according to
the relative speed of the object relative to a reference, such as
the speed of a virtual object, by a modification from relative
speed column 708. In the simplified example shown, for object
ID #1, its base sound of type 1 is modified by a modification "E" when the relative between the object and the reference is
high or fast and by a modification "F" when the relative
between the object and the reference is low or slow. It is to be
understood that more than two modification entries in the
columns 704, 706, 708 for each sound type in column 702 may
be implemented.
As described in paragraph 54 of Taylor, a sound is modified based on a speed of a virtual
object. Hence, it is not been shown that Taylor describes or suggests "haptic feedback data", as is recited in the claim 8 and 19.
Also, as explained above, it is not been shown that Taylor discloses or suggests interaction between two virtual objects. Hence, it is not been shown that Taylor teaches
"simulating a virtual interaction between the first virtual object of a video game and the second virtual object based on the type of material", as is recited in claim 9.

As per MPEP §2144.03, "It would not be appropriate for the examiner to take official notice of facts without citing a prior art reference where the facts asserted to be well known are not beyond dispute, or are not capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration as being well-known. See Ahlert, 424 F.2d at 1091, 165 USPQ at 420". As such, it is respectfully requested that the prior art reference be cited or the official notice be withdrawn.
Thus, it is respectfully requested that the section 103 rejection of claims 3 to 10, 13, 15 to 19, and 22 be withdrawn.
Claim Rejection - 35 USC § 112
Claims 1 to 22 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. §112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the enablement requirement. This rejection is respectfully traversed.

It is stated on page 8 of the office action that "[i]t is unclear how the audio data is captured. Is it captured by a microphone, sonar, or by seismic sensors?" Claim 1 is amended to include "a microphone". Figure 4A of the specification is reproduced below.

It is described in paragraph 125 of the specification with reference to Figure 4A that "[t]he microphone M3 detects sounds that are emitted from the real-world environment in which the user 7 is located. For example, as the user 7 stands up from the seat 402A or sits down on the seat 402A, a noise is created and the noise is detected by the microphone M3 to capture an audio data set p, where p is an integer". As such, a manner of capturing the audio data is by using a microphone, such as the microphone M3.

It is further stated on page 8 of the office action that "[i]s it infrasonic, within human hearing range (sonic), or ultrasonic"? Claim 1 is amended to include "sounds in the real- world environment". It is stated in paragraph 125 of the specification that "[t]he microphone M3 detects sounds that are emitted from the real-world environment". As such, all sounds, such as ones within hearing range, are detected.

It is stated on page 8 of the office action that "[i]s it passively sensing sounds in the environment, or is it actively emitting audio sounds and recording their reflected soundwaves"? As stated in paragraph 125 of the specification, the sounds are detected by the microphone M3. Figure 6 of the specification is reproduced below.

As described with reference to Figure 6, in paragraph 167, "[t]he transducer detects sound that are emitted or reflected or both from real-world objects within a real-world environment, such as the system 200 or 250 or 400 (Figures 2A, 2B, and 4), to output vibrations". Hence, as an example, the sound is detected by the transducer in a passive manner. Thus, the specification for which an example of how the "microphone" is sensing sounds in the real- world environment.

It is stated on page 8 of the office action that "[h]ow is the artificial intelligence model created and how is it used? Algorithmic steps such as those found on a flowchart, mathematical equations, or numerical criteria with physical dimensions such as constants, maxima, or minima would be helpful". It is inquired on page 8 of the office action that "[i]s the detected sound processed with analog or digital processing"? Claim 1 is amended to include "audio data in a digital format". It is stated in paragraph 167 of the specification that:

[00167] The transducer detects sound that are emitted or reflected or both from real-world objects within a real-world environment, such as the system 200 or 250 or 400 (Figures 2A, 2B, and 4), to output vibrations. The vibrations are provided to the S-E converter to modify an electrical field generated within the S-E converter to output an audio analog signal, which is an electrical signal. The audio analog signal is provided to the ADC to convert the audio analog signal from an analog form to a digital form to output an audio data set, such as the audio
data set la or lb or 2 or p (Figures 3A and 4).
(Emphasis Added)
As such, the detected sound is processed to output the audio data in the digital format.

It is further inquired on page 8 of the office action, "[w]hat physical properties of the detected materials are being measured (size, shape, volume, area, location, density, mass, temperature, etc.)"? Claim 1 does not recite "physical properties of materials". Rather, claim 1 recites "type of material". As stated in MPEP §2163, "[T]he 'essential goal' of the description of the invention requirement is to clearly convey the information that an applicant

[inventor] has invented the subject matter which is claimed." In re Barker, 559 F.2d 588, 592 n.4, 194 USPQ 470, 473 n.4 (CCPA 1977). (Emphasis Added). As such, claim 1, which recites the "subject matter which is claimed", includes "type of material" and not "physical properties". Examples of the type of material are provided in paragraph 85 of the specification, which is reproduced below.

[0085] The user 1 logs into the user account 1 and accesses the list 270. The user 1 selects one or more buttons on the input controller that is coupled to the eyeglass 218 to provide the identities, such as names, of the real-world objects, such as the seat 202A of the chair 202, the seat 204A of the chair 204, and covers of the seats 202A and 204A. Also, the user 1 selects the one or more buttons on the input controller that is coupled to the eyeglass 218 to provide the types of materials of the seats 202A and 204A, the type of material used to cover the seat 202A, and the type of material used to cover the seat 204A. For example, the user 1 selects the one or more buttons of the input controller coupled to the eyeglass 218 to spell a type of material, such as plastic, or leather, or vinyl, used for the seat 202A and selects the one or more buttons to spell a type of material used to cover of the seat 202A. As another example, the user 1 selects the one or more buttons of the input controller coupled to the eyeglass 218 to spell that that the seat 202A is a
seat of an office chair and the seat 204A is a seat of a sofa.
(Emphasis Added)

It is stated in paragraph 85 that "the user 1 selects the one or more buttons of the input controller coupled to the eyeglass 218 to spell a type of material, such as plastic, or leather, or vinyl, used for the seat 202A and selects the one or more buttons to spell a type of material used to cover of the seat 202A". As such, plastic, vinyl, and leather are each an example of a type of material. The specification, in paragraph 85, provides examples of the "type of material".

It is further stated on page 8 of the office action that "[w]hat type of artificial intelligence is being used (analytic, functional, interactive, text, or visual; reactive machine, limited memory, theory of mind, self-aware, artificial narrow intelligence, artificial general intelligence, or artificial superintelligence)"? The specification provides an example of the artificial intelligence model. As stated in paragraph 54 of the present patent application, "[i]n an embodiment, the AI model is sometimes referred to herein as a machine learning model" As such, an example of the AI model is the machine learning model. Hence, the specification provides various examples for enabling the recitations of claim 1.

For the same reasons set forth above, the specification provides various examples for enabling the recitations of claim 11 and 20. Hence, the independent claims 11 and 20 are submitted to satisfy the enablement requirement. Also, claims 2-9 depend from independent claim 1, claims 12-19 depend from independent claim 11, and claims 21 and 22 depend from independent claim 20. Hence, for the same reasons set forth above with respect to the independent claims 1, 11, and 20, the respective dependent claims 2-9, 12-19, 21, and 22 satisfy the enablement requirement.
Therefore, it is respectfully requested that the section 112 rejection of claims 1-22 for lacking enablement be withdrawn.
Claim Rejection - 35 USC § 112

Claims 1 to 22 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) or 35 U.S.C. §112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre- AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention. This rejection is respectfully traversed.

As explained above with respect to the enablement requirement, the specification provides various examples of the recitations of claim 1. Hence, for the same reasons set forth above, claim 1 is submitted to be definite.
Also, for the same reasons set forth above, the specification provides various examples of the recitations of claim 11 and 20. Hence, the independent claims 11 and 20 are submitted to be definite.

Claims 2-9 depend from independent claim 1, claims 12-19 depend from independent claim 11, and claims 21 and 22 depend from independent claim 20. Hence, for the same reasons set forth above with respect to the independent claims 1, 11, and 20, the respective dependent claims 2-9, 12-19, 21, and 22 are submitted to be definite.
Thus, it is respectfully requested that the section 112 indefiniteness rejection of claims 1-22 be withdrawn.
A Notice of Allowance is respectfully requested.
